Apple.explanation: Apples come in red, green, and yellow and are very healthy
points: Over 7,500 known apple varieties exist worldwide
Apples float due to 25% air volume inside
One medium apple provides about 4–5 grams of dietary fiber
Rich in quercetin, an antioxidant supporting heart and lung health
The phrase 'an apple a day keeps the doctor away' has roots in 19th-century Wales

Banana.explanation: Bananas are yellow when ripe and give you lots of energy
points: Bananas are botanically berries; strawberries are not
Contain natural sugars, potassium, and vitamin B6 for quick and sustained energy
Banana plants are giant herbs, not trees
Help regulate blood pressure thanks to high potassium content
Most commercial bananas are the Cavendish variety

Mango.explanation: Mangoes are called the King of Fruits and taste delicious
points: Mangoes belong to the same family as cashews and poison ivy
India produces about 40% of the world's mangoes
Very high in vitamins A and C — great for eyes and immunity
Over 1,000 mango cultivars exist globally
Unripe green mangoes are used in chutneys and pickles

Strawberry.explanation: Strawberries are red, sweet, and shaped like a little heart
points: The seeds are on the outside — an average berry has about 200
Strawberries contain more vitamin C (per gram) than oranges
Not true berries botanically — they are aggregate accessory fruits
High in anthocyanins, supporting brain and heart health
The aroma comes from over 50 different flavor compounds

Watermelon.explanation: Watermelons are mostly water and very refreshing in summer
points: 92–95% water — excellent natural hydration source
Contains citrulline, which converts to arginine and improves blood flow
Native to northeast Africa; ancient Egyptians placed them in tombs
Yellow- and orange-fleshed varieties exist alongside red
The heaviest recorded watermelon weighed over 350 pounds (159 kg)

Grapes.explanation: Grapes grow in big bunches and can be red or green
points: One of the oldest cultivated crops — evidence from 8,000 years ago
Red and purple grapes contain resveratrol, linked to heart health
Used for wine, raisins, juice, jelly, and fresh eating
Seedless grapes were created through natural mutation and breeding
A single vine can produce 10–20 pounds of grapes annually

Orange.explanation: Oranges are full of Vitamin C which keeps us healthy
points: One medium orange supplies over 100% of daily vitamin C needs
Originally green in tropical climates; turn orange only in cooler weather
The sweet orange we eat today originated in China
Florida and Brazil are the top orange juice–producing regions
Peel oils are used in perfumes, cleaners, and flavorings

Pineapple.explanation: Pineapples have a spiky crown and grow on low plants near the ground
points: A pineapple is actually a multiple fruit formed from 100–200 flowers
Contains bromelain — an enzyme that tenderizes meat and aids digestion
Takes 18–24 months to grow and ripen
Named because it resembles a pine cone
Never ripens further after harvest — must be picked ripe

Cherry.explanation: Cherries are tiny red fruits that grow in pairs on trees
points: Cherries are drupes (stone fruits) related to plums and peaches
Contain melatonin — may help improve sleep quality
There are over 1,000 cherry varieties — sweet and sour types
Japan celebrates cherry blossom season (sakura) with great cultural importance
The pits contain cyanogenic compounds (but are rarely toxic in small amounts)

Kiwi.explanation: Kiwi fruits are brown outside and bright green inside
points: Originally called Chinese gooseberry; renamed kiwi in New Zealand
One kiwi provides more vitamin C than an orange
The fuzzy skin is edible and contains extra fiber and nutrients
Actinidin enzyme can tenderize meat (similar to papaya and pineapple)
Gold and baby kiwi varieties are now common in stores

Peach.explanation: Peaches have fuzzy skin and sweet juicy flesh inside
points: Peaches and nectarines are the same species — nectarines are smooth-skinned mutants
Symbol of longevity and immortality in Chinese culture
Rich in vitamins A and C plus antioxidants
The pit (stone) is almond-like and related to almonds
Georgia (USA) is nicknamed the Peach State

Pear.explanation: Pears are shaped like teardrops and are sweet and juicy
points: Pears ripen from the inside out — best to ripen at room temperature
One of the oldest cultivated fruits — mentioned in Homer’s Odyssey
High in fiber, especially in the skin
Over 3,000 known pear varieties worldwide
European pears (Bartlett) and Asian pears (crisp like apples) are main types

Lemon.explanation: Lemons are very sour and full of Vitamin C
points: Lemons were used by British sailors to prevent scurvy (hence 'limey')
Citric acid gives lemons their sour taste and preserves food
Lemon zest contains the most intense flavor (essential oils)
One lemon provides about 31 mg of vitamin C
Widely used in cleaning, beauty, and culinary applications

Lime.explanation: Limes are small green citrus fruits used in drinks and cooking
points: Limes are more acidic than lemons — key in margaritas and ceviche
Key limes are smaller and more aromatic than Persian (Tahiti) limes
Help prevent scurvy like lemons in naval history
Rich in flavonoids and vitamin C
Lime juice can curdle coconut milk in some traditional dishes

Coconut.explanation: Coconuts are large tropical fruits full of refreshing water inside
points: Coconuts are drupes — not true nuts
Coconut water is naturally sterile and used in IV drips in emergencies
All parts are used: water, flesh, oil, husk, shell, coir
Coconut palms can live 60–100 years and produce fruit continuously
Classified botanically as a fruit, not a nut

Papaya.explanation: Papayas are tropical fruits with orange flesh and black seeds
points: Contain papain enzyme — used commercially as meat tenderizer
One of the highest vitamin C fruits per serving
Seeds are edible — peppery when dried and ground
Native to Central America; now grown in most tropical regions
Green papaya is used in salads (som tam in Thailand)

Blueberry.explanation: Blueberries are tiny blue berries packed with powerful antioxidants
points: Rank among the highest antioxidant foods (especially wild varieties)
Support brain health — may delay age-related cognitive decline
Native to North America — commercial cultivation began in early 1900s
Low glycemic index — good for blood sugar control
High in anthocyanins, giving the blue color

Raspberry.explanation: Raspberries are delicate red berries that grow on thorny bushes
points: One of the highest-fiber fruits per calorie
Rich in ellagic acid — studied for potential anti-cancer properties
Come in red, black, purple, and golden varieties
Very fragile — usually harvested by hand
Leaves are used in herbal tea for centuries

Blackberry.explanation: Blackberries are dark purple berries that grow wild in hedgerows
points: Wild blackberries often sweeter than cultivated ones
High in vitamin C, K, manganese, and fiber
Historically used as natural dye and in folk medicine
Related to raspberries — aggregate fruit structure
Thorns protect the plant from herbivores

Plum.explanation: Plums are juicy purple fruits that can be dried to make prunes
points: Dried plums (prunes) are well-known for promoting digestive health
Contain sorbitol — a natural laxative
Over 2,000 plum varieties worldwide
Japanese and European plums are the two main types
Rich in vitamin K and antioxidants

Pomegranate.explanation: Pomegranates are filled with hundreds of tiny red jewel-like seeds
points: One fruit can contain 200–1,400 arils (juice sacs)
Ancient symbol of fertility, prosperity, and eternal life
Very high in punicalagins — powerful antioxidants
Mentioned in Egyptian mythology, Bible, and Quran
Arils are the edible part; rind and membranes are bitter

Guava.explanation: Guavas have pink flesh and are extremely rich in Vitamin C
points: One guava can contain 4× more vitamin C than an orange
Both skin and seeds are edible
Used in traditional medicine for diarrhea and digestion
Strong tropical aroma when ripe
High in lycopene (especially pink varieties)

Lychee.explanation: Lychees have a bumpy pink shell and a sweet white fruit inside
points: Part of the soapberry family — related to rambutan and longan
Floral, grape-like flavor with rose notes
Very high in vitamin C when fresh
Popular in Chinese desserts and fresh eating
Shell peels easily when ripe

Dragonfruit.explanation: Dragon fruit has a bright pink skin with white speckled flesh inside
points: Grows on climbing cactus plants (Hylocereus species)
Low-calorie, high-fiber, and contains vitamin C
Mild flavor — often compared to kiwi + pear
Yellow-skinned varieties are usually sweeter
Rich in betalains (antioxidants from the skin)

Passion Fruit.explanation: Passion fruits have a wrinkly purple shell and tangy yellow seeds inside
points: Wrinkled skin = fully ripe and sweetest
Seeds are edible and add crunch
High in vitamins A and C plus fiber
Name comes from passion flower resembling crucifixion symbols
Used widely in juices, desserts, and cocktails

Fig.explanation: Figs are one of the oldest cultivated fruits in human history
points: Figs are inverted flowers (syconium) — not true fruit
No visible pollination needed for common edible figs
High in fiber, potassium, and calcium
Mentioned in ancient Egyptian, Greek, and Biblical texts
Dried figs are energy-dense and long-lasting

Date.explanation: Dates are very sweet sticky fruits that grow on palm trees
points: One of the oldest cultivated tree crops — over 6,000 years
Very high in natural sugars — excellent quick energy
Rich in potassium, magnesium, and fiber
Important staple food in Middle East and North Africa
Medjool dates are large, soft, and premium

Apricot.explanation: Apricots are small orange fruits similar to peaches but less fuzzy
points: Very high in beta-carotene (vitamin A precursor)
Originated in China over 4,000 years ago
Dried apricots are popular snacks and rich in iron
Short fresh season — often preserved
Related to plums, peaches, and almonds

Grapefruit.explanation: Grapefruits are large citrus fruits with a bitter sweet taste
points: Accidental hybrid between pomelo and sweet orange
Pink and red varieties contain lycopene
Can interact with many medications (CYP3A4 inhibition)
High in vitamin C and fiber
Named because fruits grow in grape-like clusters

Tangerine.explanation: Tangerines are small easy-to-peel oranges with a sweet flavor
points: Easier to peel than oranges — loose skin
Clementines and mandarins are tangerine types
High in vitamin C and natural sweetness
Small size makes them perfect portable snacks
Sweeter and less acidic than standard oranges

Cantaloupe.explanation: Cantaloupes are round melons with orange flesh and a sweet fragrance
points: Very high in vitamin A (beta-carotene)
Hydrating — about 90% water
Netted rind distinguishes it from smooth-skinned melons
Rich in potassium and folate
Best when fragrant at the stem end

Honeydew.explanation: Honeydew melons have pale green flesh and are very sweet
points: Smooth rind — no netting like cantaloupe
High water content — excellent for hydration
Mild, sweet flavor pairs well with salty foods (e.g., prosciutto)
Good source of vitamin C and potassium
Part of the muskmelon family

Starfruit.explanation: When you cut a starfruit sideways it makes a perfect star shape
points: Also called carambola
Waxy edible skin
Tart-sweet taste — green apple + grape + citrus notes
High in vitamin C and low in calories
Caution: high oxalic acid — avoid in large amounts if kidney issues

Jackfruit.explanation: Jackfruit is the largest fruit that grows on a tree, sometimes over 80 pounds
points: World’s largest tree-borne fruit
Unripe flesh used as vegan meat substitute (pulled pork texture)
Ripe fruit is sweet and tropical
Native to South and Southeast Asia
Seeds can be boiled or roasted like nuts

Durian.explanation: Durian is called the King of Tropical Fruits but has a very strong smell
points: Banned on public transport in Singapore and some places due to odor
Custard-like flesh with divisive flavor (onion-caramel-almond mix)
High in nutrients but very calorie-dense
Often paired with mangosteen (king & queen of fruits)
Spiky husk protects creamy interior

Rambutan.explanation: Rambutans are hairy red fruits related to lychees and very sweet inside
points: Name means 'hairy' in Malay
Sweet, juicy, translucent flesh similar to lychee
High in vitamin C
Related to lychee, longan, and ackee
Hairy shell peels easily when ripe

Longan.explanation: Longans are called Dragon Eye fruit and taste like sweet honey
points: Name means 'dragon eye' in Chinese (due to seed appearance)
Smaller and milder than lychee
Dried longans used in Chinese herbal teas
Grows in clusters like grapes
Sweet with subtle floral-honey notes

Tamarind.explanation: Tamarind is a sour brown pod fruit used in cooking and drinks worldwide
points: Key ingredient in Worcestershire sauce, pad thai, and chutneys
High in tartaric acid — strong sour flavor
Rich in antioxidants, magnesium, and iron
Sticky pulp surrounds hard seeds
Ancient African fruit now grown throughout tropics

Mulberry.explanation: Mulberries look like elongated blackberries and stain your fingers purple
points: Used for centuries to feed silkworms (white mulberry)
Stain very easily — natural dye source
High in vitamin C, iron, and antioxidants
Sweet-tart flavor; white, red, and black varieties
Berries fall when ripe — often collected by shaking tree

Elderberry.explanation: Elderberries are dark purple berries used in syrups and medicine
points: Raw berries, leaves, and stems are toxic — must be cooked
Popular in cold & flu remedies (high in antioxidants)
Used in wines, jams, pies, and cordials
Elder flowers are edible and used in drinks
Native to many temperate regions

Gooseberry.explanation: Gooseberries are small tart berries that grow on spiny bushes
points: Very tart when green — sweeter when ripe (red/purple)
High in vitamin C and pectin — great for jams
Related to currants
Spiny bushes make harvesting challenging
Popular in British cuisine (gooseberry fool, pies)

Persimmon.explanation: Persimmons are bright orange fruits that taste like honey when very ripe
points: Astringent (astringent) and non-astringent (Fuyu) types
Astringent varieties must be very soft before eating
High in vitamins A, C, and fiber
Native to China — national fruit of Japan
Dried persimmons (hoshigaki) are a traditional delicacy

Kumquat.explanation: Kumquats are tiny orange fruits you eat whole including the sweet skin
points: Edible skin is sweet; flesh is tart — eaten whole
Smallest citrus fruit commonly eaten
High in vitamin C and fiber (especially skin)
Used in marmalades and liqueurs
Symbol of good luck in Chinese New Year

Quince.explanation: Quinces are golden yellow fruits too hard to eat raw but wonderful cooked
points: Very hard and astringent raw — must be cooked
Strong floral aroma when cooked
High in pectin — used in jams, jellies, and membrillo paste
Ancient fruit mentioned in Greek and Roman texts
Related to apples and pears

Breadfruit.explanation: Breadfruit got its name because its starchy flesh tastes like freshly baked bread
points: Starchy texture when cooked — used like potato or bread
High in carbohydrates, low in fat
Captain Bligh’s voyage on the Bounty was to transport breadfruit
Can be roasted, boiled, fried, or made into flour
Important staple in Pacific Islands

Nectarine.explanation: Nectarines are like peaches but with smooth shiny skin instead of fuzzy
points: Smooth-skinned genetic variant of peach
Same nutritional profile as peaches
Often slightly smaller and more aromatic
Skin is edible and adds texture
Popular in summer fruit salads

Ugli Fruit.explanation: Ugli fruit has a wrinkled ugly outside but a sweet delicious inside
points: Hybrid between grapefruit, orange, and tangerine
Thick, loose skin peels very easily
Sweet-tart flavor — less bitter than grapefruit
Name comes from 'ugly' appearance
Grown mainly in Jamaica

Ackee.explanation: Ackee is the national fruit of Jamaica and must be ripe before eating safely
points: Unripe ackee contains hypoglycin A — toxic if eaten raw/immature
National fruit of Jamaica; used in ackee & saltfish dish
Soft, creamy flesh when ripe
Related to lychee and longan
Must be fully open and ripe before consumption

Cherimoya.explanation: Cherimoya is called the custard apple because its flesh is creamy and sweet
points: Mark Twain called it 'the most delicious fruit known to man'
Custard-like texture and sweet tropical flavor
Seeds are toxic — remove before eating
High in vitamin C and B vitamins
Native to Andes mountains

Soursop.explanation: Soursop has a spiky green skin and a creamy white interior with a tangy flavor
points: Also called graviola
Used in traditional medicine (especially for cancer claims — not proven)
Flavor like pineapple-strawberry mix
Large fruit with soft spines
Leaves used for herbal tea

Carambola.explanation: Carambola is another name for starfruit which makes star shapes when sliced
points: Cross-section naturally forms a perfect star
Waxy edible skin
Tart-sweet — green apple, grape, citrus notes
High vitamin C, low calories
Caution: high oxalates — limit if kidney stones risk

Feijoa.explanation: Feijoas smell like tropical perfume and taste like a mix of guava and mint
points: Also called pineapple guava
Strong sweet aroma — pineapple, guava, mint mix
Edible sweet skin; jelly-like flesh
Native to South America, popular in New Zealand
High in vitamin C and fiber

Mangosteen.explanation: Mangosteen is called the Queen of Fruits with a sweet tangy white interior
points: Paired with durian as Queen to durian’s King
Thick purple rind; delicate white segments inside
Very high in xanthones — powerful antioxidants
Sweet-tart flavor — often described as divine
Hard to grow outside Southeast Asia

Salak.explanation: Salak is called snake fruit because of its scaly brown skin
points: Scaly brown skin resembles snake skin
Tart-sweet apple-like flesh with astringent notes
Hard brown pit inside
Popular street food in Indonesia
Grows in clusters at base of palm

Sapodilla.explanation: Sapodilla tastes like a pear soaked in brown sugar and caramel
points: Source of chicle — original chewing gum base
Caramel-pear-brown sugar flavor when ripe
High in fiber and vitamin C
Native to Central America
Latex used historically for gum

Cupuaçu.explanation: Cupuaçu is a South American fruit related to cacao with a creamy white pulp
points: Close relative of cacao (chocolate tree)
Creamy pulp used in desserts and juices
Strong chocolate-pineapple-pear flavor
Seeds used to make cupuaçu butter
Very popular in Brazil and Amazon region

Miracle Fruit.explanation: Miracle fruit makes sour foods taste sweet after you eat it
points: Miraculin protein binds to taste buds — alters sour perception
Turns lemons, limes, vinegar taste sweet for 30–60 minutes
Used in 'flavor-tripping' experiences
West African origin
Potential for low-sugar products

Pitahaya.explanation: Pitahaya is a yellow dragon fruit even sweeter than the pink variety
points: Yellow variety usually sweeter than pink/red
Grows on cactus — same family as dragon fruit
High in fiber, vitamin C, and iron
Mild kiwi-pear flavor
Antioxidants from vibrant skin

Pomelo.explanation: Pomelos are the largest citrus fruit in the world with thick fluffy rind
points: Largest citrus — can weigh up to 10 kg (22 lb)
Ancestor of grapefruit
Mild, sweet flavor — less acidic than grapefruit
Thick rind used in candied peel
Symbol of prosperity in Chinese culture

Buddha's Hand.explanation: Buddha's Hand citrus fruit has finger-like segments and smells amazing
points: No juice or pulp — mostly rind
Strong citron aroma — used as natural air freshener
Symbol of happiness, longevity, and good fortune
Common in Chinese New Year decorations
Rind used in desserts, liqueurs, and perfumes

Calamansi.explanation: Calamansi are tiny citrus fruits popular in Southeast Asian cooking
points: Hybrid between kumquat and mandarin
Very sour — used like lime/lemon
Popular in Filipino, Malaysian, Indonesian dishes
Whole fruit often squeezed into drinks
High vitamin C content

Cloudberry.explanation: Cloudberries grow in Arctic regions and are golden orange when ripe
points: Golden-orange 'Arctic gold' berry
Grows in northern bogs and tundra
High in vitamin C and ellagic acid
Used in Scandinavian liqueurs and jams
Delicate and expensive due to wild harvesting

Boysenberry.explanation: Boysenberries are a cross between raspberries, blackberries, and loganberries
points: Hybrid created by Rudolph Boysen in 1920s
Large, juicy, tart-sweet flavor
Used in jams, syrups, desserts
Dark purple when fully ripe
Higher vitamin C than many berries

Acerola.explanation: Acerola cherries have 65 times more Vitamin C than oranges
points: Highest natural vitamin C source of any fruit
Also called Barbados cherry or West Indian cherry
Small, bright red, very tart
Used in supplements and fortification
Native to Central and South America

Pitanga.explanation: Pitanga is a Brazilian cherry also called Surinam cherry with a ridged shape
points: Ridged, star-like appearance
Ranges from sweet to tart depending on variety
High in vitamin C and lycopene
Used in jellies, juices, and ice cream
Grows on fast-growing shrub

Cactus Pear.explanation: Cactus pears grow on cacti and have a sweet red or yellow flesh inside
points: Also called prickly pear or tuna
Grows on Opuntia cactus pads
Sweet, melon-like flavor with many seeds
High in fiber, vitamin C, magnesium
Spines must be removed before eating

Jabuticaba.explanation: Jabuticaba is a unique fruit that grows directly on the trunk of the tree
points: Cauliflory — fruit grows directly on trunk and branches
Grape-like dark purple berries
Sweet with slight tartness
Popular in Brazil — eaten fresh or in jelly/wine
Tree can produce multiple crops per year

Marula.explanation: Marula fruits ferment on the tree and animals get tipsy eating them
points: Ferments naturally on tree — animals reportedly get drunk
Used to make Amarula cream liqueur
High in vitamin C and antioxidants
Native to southern Africa
Both fruit and nut (kernel) are used

Bael.explanation: Bael fruit has a hard woody shell and a fragrant sticky pulp inside
points: Hard woody shell — eaten fresh or dried
Used in traditional Ayurvedic medicine
Sweet, aromatic, slightly astringent pulp
Sacred tree in Hinduism
Made into sherbet drink in India

Monstera Fruit.explanation: Monstera deliciosa fruit takes over a year to ripen and tastes like pineapple
points: Also called ceriman or Swiss cheese plant fruit
Takes 12+ months to fully ripen
Pineapple-banana-coconut flavor when ripe
Unripe fruit contains calcium oxalate — causes burning sensation
Rarely sold commercially due to long ripening time

Rose Apple.explanation: Rose apples are shaped like bells and have a faint rose aroma
points: Bell-shaped with thin skin
Crisp, juicy, mildly sweet with rose fragrance
Eaten fresh or used in salads
Common in Southeast Asia and India
Seeds are toxic if chewed

Wax Apple.explanation: Wax apples look shiny and artificial but are real crunchy fruits
points: Shiny, waxy skin — bell-shaped
Crisp, juicy, mildly sweet
Popular in Taiwan, Malaysia, India
Eaten fresh or pickled
Related to rose apple

Loquat.explanation: Loquats are small golden fruits that grow in clusters and taste sweet-tart
points: Also called Japanese plum
Sweet-tart, peach-apricot flavor
High in vitamin A and fiber
Leaves used in herbal teas
Early spring fruit in many regions

Jujube.explanation: Jujubes are small red fruits also called Chinese dates full of Vitamin C
points: Also called Chinese date or red date
High in vitamin C — more than citrus per weight
Eaten fresh, dried, or candied
Used in Chinese herbal medicine
Dried jujubes are sweet and chewy

Pawpaw.explanation: Pawpaws are North America's largest native fruit tasting like mango custard
points: Largest edible fruit native to North America
Custard-like texture — mango-banana-pineapple flavor
Short shelf life — rarely sold commercially
Pollinated by flies and beetles (not bees)
Rich in vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants

Langsat.explanation: Langsats grow in grape-like clusters and taste sweet with a hint of grapefruit
points: Grows in clusters like grapes
Sweet with slight tart grapefruit note
Translucent flesh around seed
Popular in Southeast Asia
Related to longkong and duku varieties

Mamey Sapote.explanation: Mamey sapote has pinkish-orange flesh that tastes like sweet potato and almond
points: Sweet potato–almond–chocolate flavor
Large fruit with rough brown skin
Used in milkshakes, ice cream, smoothies
Native to Mexico and Central America
High in vitamin C and fiber

Ilama.explanation: Ilamas are tropical fruits related to cherimoya with green or pink skin
points: Close relative of cherimoya and soursop
Sweet, creamy white flesh
Pink or green skin varieties
Rare outside Central America
Seeds are toxic

Pummelo.explanation: Pummelos are ancient citrus ancestors of the modern grapefruit
points: Largest citrus fruit — ancestor of grapefruit
Thick, spongy rind
Mild, sweet, less acidic than grapefruit
Popular in Southeast Asia
Used in pomelo salads

Natal Plum.explanation: Natal plums are red star-shaped fruits from South Africa with a sweet-tart taste
points: Star-shaped when viewed from top
Sweet-tart cranberry-like flavor
High in vitamin C
Used in jams and sauces
Grows on thorny shrub

Ice Cream Bean.explanation: Ice cream beans are long pods filled with cotton candy-like white pulp
points: Sweet, cotton-candy-like pulp around seeds
Pods can be 1 meter long
Popular street food in Central/South America
Seeds are not eaten
Tree fixes nitrogen in soil

Rollinia.explanation: Rollinia is a tropical fruit with a bumpy yellow skin and lemony cream flesh
points: Bumpy yellow skin when ripe
Creamy, lemony-sweet flesh
Related to cherimoya
Fragile — hard to transport
Popular in Brazil and Peru

Black Sapote.explanation: Black sapote is nicknamed the chocolate pudding fruit for its dark rich flesh
points: Dark brown-black flesh when ripe
Texture and flavor like chocolate pudding
Used in desserts and smoothies
Related to persimmon
High in vitamin C

Canistel.explanation: Canistel is called the egg fruit because its dry yellow flesh resembles egg yolk
points: Bright yellow, dry, egg-yolk-like flesh
Sweet, rich, pumpkin-like flavor
Used in milkshakes and custards
Native to Central America
High in carotenoids

Abiu.explanation: Abiu is a yellow tropical fruit from the Amazon with translucent sweet flesh
points: Translucent, milky-sweet flesh
Very sticky latex in skin — eat carefully
Caramel-vanilla flavor
Popular in Amazon and Brazil
High in vitamin C

Mamoncillo.explanation: Mamoncillo is a small green fruit you pop open to reveal a tangy pink pulp
points: Also called Spanish lime or quenepa
Sweet-tart jelly-like pulp around large seed
Eaten by sucking pulp off seed
Popular street snack in Caribbean and Latin America
High in calcium and phosphorus

Genip.explanation: Genips are tropical fruits with firm green skin and sweet orange flesh
points: Same as mamoncillo/Spanish lime
Sweet-tangy orange pulp
Popular in Puerto Rico, Dominican Republic
Eaten fresh by popping open
Kids favorite street fruit

Jabara.explanation: Jabara is a rare Japanese citrus from Wakayama with a unique bitter-sweet flavor
points: Rare citrus grown mainly in Wakayama, Japan
Bitter-sweet, aromatic flavor
Used in traditional Japanese medicine
High in flavonoids
Very limited production

Kiwano.explanation: Kiwano is a horned melon from Africa with bright orange skin and green jelly inside
points: Also called horned melon or African horned cucumber
Vibrant orange spiky skin
Green jelly flesh with seeds — cucumber-banana-lime flavor
High in vitamin C and water
Used in fruit salads and drinks

Noni.explanation: Noni fruit has a strong smell but is used as traditional medicine across the Pacific
points: Very strong, pungent smell — often called 'cheese fruit'
Used in Polynesian traditional medicine for centuries
High in antioxidants and vitamin C
Juice marketed as health supplement
Eaten ripe or drunk as juice

Tamarillo.explanation: Tamarillos are also called tree tomatoes and are eaten with a spoon
points: Also called tree tomato
Egg-shaped with red, orange, or yellow skin
Tart flesh — eaten with spoon like kiwi
High in vitamin C and A
Popular in New Zealand and South America

Naranjilla.explanation: Naranjilla is a South American fruit with a tart citrusy flavor like lime and rhubarb
points: Name means 'little orange' in Spanish
Hairy green-orange skin when ripe
Tart, lime-rhubarb-pineapple flavor
Used in juices and desserts in Colombia, Ecuador
High in vitamin C and iron

Pepino.explanation: Pepino melon is a South American fruit that tastes like a mix of melon and cucumber
points: Also called sweet cucumber
Mild, sweet, melon-cucumber flavor
Purple-striped skin when ripe
Low calorie and high water content
Popular in Peru, Chile, New Zealand

Davidson Plum.explanation: Davidson plums are Australian native fruits with deep purple skin and tart red flesh
points: Very tart — used in sauces, jams, desserts
Extremely high in antioxidants
Native to rainforests of Australia
Deep purple flesh stains heavily
Superfood status in recent years

Finger Lime.explanation: Finger limes are called citrus caviar because the flesh pops in tiny juice pearls
points: Tiny juice vesicles pop like caviar
Called 'citrus caviar' or 'Australian caviar'
Lime, lemon, grapefruit flavors depending on variety
Very expensive and sought after by chefs
Native to Australian rainforests

Uva Ursi.explanation: Uva ursi or bearberry produces small red fruits eaten by bears and birds
points: Also called bearberry
Small red berries eaten by wildlife
Leaves used in herbal medicine (urinary tract)
Berries are mealy and bland for humans
Common in northern temperate zones

Sea Buckthorn.explanation: Sea buckthorn berries are extremely sour orange berries rich in Vitamin C
points: Very high in vitamin C — more than oranges
Bright orange berries on thorny shrubs
Used in juices, oils, supplements
Grows in harsh coastal and mountain areas
Rich in omega-7 fatty acids

Barberry.explanation: Barberries are tiny tart red berries used in Persian rice dishes and jams
points: Very tart — used dried in Persian cuisine (zereshk)
Common in saffron rice dishes
High in berberine — studied for health benefits
Thorny shrub — related to Oregon grape
Used in jams and sauces

Hackberry.explanation: Hackberries are small purple-brown wild berries with a sweet date-like flavor
points: Sweet date-nut flavor when ripe
Small, hard pit inside
Used by Native Americans historically
Tree common in North America
Berries persist on tree into winter

Salmonberry.explanation: Salmonberries are Pacific Northwest berries ranging from yellow to deep red
points: Range from pale yellow to deep salmon-red
Important food for Pacific Northwest indigenous peoples
Mild, slightly tart flavor
Often eaten with salmon — hence name
Related to raspberries and blackberries
